entry.evidence: This study evaluates the potential of Sentinel-1 (S-1) synthetic aperture radar (SAR) time series for monitoring SC depletion and snowmelt

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML (jats_text), with PDF for figure pages

steps.action: Framed the gap: snow cover distribution and melt timing are poorly known at small spatiotemporal scales in the Arctic.
steps.quote: knowledge about SC distribution is still limited, especially at small spatiotemporal scales

steps.action: Took up the freely available Sentinel-1 C-band SAR mission (10-20 m, 6 d repeat) as a cloud- and illumination-independent capability.
steps.quote: SAR data have become an attractive alternative

steps.action: Adopted the seasonal backscatter model of Marin et al. (2020) and its three rival explanations of the runoff-phase backscatter increase (surface roughness, grains or ice lenses, subpixel snow-free fraction).
steps.quote: This steady increase is not fully understood yet, but three possible explanation are described by

steps.action: Proposed a new approach that adapts Nagler's method to the seasonal SAR evolution, using seasonal-minimum thresholds and the backscatter derivative.
steps.quote: We here propose a novel approach, which adapts Nagler’s method

steps.action: Acquired all IW SLC dual-pol S-1 scenes for 2017-2018 over Zackenberg (97) and Kobbefjord (94), plus daily time-lapse camera images, screening out bad-quality images.
steps.quote: we investigated all S-1 single look complex (SLC) data interferometric wide swath mode (IW) acquisitions

steps.action: Preprocessed S-1 scenes to terrain-flattened gamma0 stacks at 20 m following the coauthors' earlier workflow.
steps.quote: The processing of S-1 products followed the workflow developed in

steps.action: Built the algorithm: SOR at the seasonal minimum, EOS by threshold above the minimum or by the temporally filtered derivative, an end-of-season snow class (9 dB HV autumn rule), and binary SC maps per date.
steps.quote: we also implement an approach using the derivative of the backscatter time series to detect EOS

steps.action: Built the reference product: aligned, classified and orthorectified time-lapse images into 2.5 m SC maps aggregated to 20 m SC fraction, with camera-based EOS, SOD and EOD.
steps.quote: Orthorectified SC maps are generated from time-lapse camera images to validate the S-1 EOS and SC products

steps.action: Checked the reference against ground control points (RMSE 9.4 m and 5.3 m) and against GeoBasis in situ SC fraction from the same camera (R2 0.98, RMSE 3.7 %).
steps.quote: The correlation of in situ SC fraction and mean SC fraction of the orthorectified SC fraction maps is tested

steps.action: Designed the evaluation: a backscatter-versus-SC-fraction interaction analysis relative to SOD/EOD, and same-day accuracy assessment (confusion matrix, ROC, EOS R2/RMSE/MAE, offset histograms) across threshold ranges and both polarizations.
steps.quote: we investigated a threshold range from 2 to 8 dB for HV and from 2 to 10 dB for HH polarization

steps.action: Established that in Zackenberg backscatter rises sharply 10-15 d before SC fraction starts to fall, in both years and polarizations, then rises linearly during SC decrease; in Kobbefjord almost no pre-SOD rise.
steps.quote: A sharp increase in intensity within the last 10–15 d before SOD

steps.action: Varied threshold and polarization: higher t overestimates start-of-season snow-free areas and lower t detects EOS too early; the optimum depends on polarization, year and site; HV is more stable.
steps.quote: the t values for the best results depend on the used polarization and the observed year and site

steps.action: Compared the derivative-based EOS with the threshold-based EOS on the same data: the derivative adapts to differing optimal thresholds, with small EOS offsets in ZRA and +5 to +7 d in KRA.
steps.quote: The derivative approach adapts to differences in optimal thresholds

steps.action: Compared S-1 SC maps (HV, 4 dB, and derivative) with same-day camera maps: overall accuracy always above 75 %; EOS R2 0.41 (threshold) and 0.63 (derivative) in ZRA, R2 below 0 in KRA.
steps.quote: overall accuracy is always above 75 % and in more than half of the cases above 90 %

steps.action: Posed rivals for the missing pre-SOD increase in Kobbefjord (morning acquisition time versus faster, patchier snow depletion) and attributed the HV rise to depolarization at a rougher surface.
steps.quote: could be either due to the different acquisition time in the morning but is more likely caused by systematic differences in SC distribution

steps.action: Used the SOD-to-EOD duration (about 10 d in ZRA, more than 20 d in KRA) as evidence favouring the snow-distribution explanation.
steps.quote: the temporal difference between SOD and EOD, which is about 10 d in ZRA but more than 20 d in KRA

steps.action: Kept the interpretation that snowpack change and decreasing fractional SC jointly drive the runoff-phase backscatter increase.
steps.quote: These results are of comparably high validity, as the observations have been compared to a high-resolution reference dataset

steps.action: Explained the weaker 2017 ROC and the year-to-year shift of optimal thresholds by auxiliaries (short or gappy time series, snow depth, acquisition time) rather than revising the method.
steps.quote: could be caused by the limited length of the time series in ZRA and gaps in the time series in KRA

steps.action: Generalized across sites: the approach works at a high-Arctic and a low-Arctic site with different orbits and acquisition times.
steps.quote: our case study shows that our approach works well with both settings as different orbits (ascending in ZRA and descending in KRA)

steps.action: Set the accuracies against published optical SC mapping and the Tsai et al. supervised SAR classification, finding comparable accuracy at higher resolution, independent of clouds.
steps.quote: accuracies comparable to other latest SC mapping approaches using optical remote sensing with similar spatial resolution

steps.action: Concluded that S-1 time series map SC depletion and EOS at 20 m and 6 d; HV with a 4 dB global threshold or the derivative gives overall accuracy above 75 %; transferability is still to be confirmed.
steps.quote: Using the derivative instead produced similar results and adapts well to different environmental settings [...] .

sequences.source_document: Open discussion of preprint tc-2021-78 (RC1-RC4, AC1-AC4)

steps.action: After RC1 (¶5-¶7) and RC4 questioned transferability beyond Zackenberg, added Kobbefjord as a second site and repeated all camera and S-1 processing there.
steps.quote: We have included a second test site and now show results also for the Kobbefjord region

steps.action: After RC3 (¶5) recommended thresholding the temporal derivative instead of a fixed 4 dB threshold, added the derivative-based EOS approach.
steps.quote: We followed your advice and we have now included an approach that uses the derivatives of the time series

steps.action: Declined RC1 (¶6) and RC3 (¶8) requests to use EW mode or several orbits; added only a discussion statement.
steps.quote: As such we have not considered the use of EW data

steps.action: Declined RC1 (¶9) request to test coarser resolution (50-100 m) to reduce speckle.
steps.quote: However, we wanted to make use of the high-resolution in situ camera imagery and the Sentinel-1 IW data.

steps.action: Declined RC1 (¶10) request to analyse local incidence angle as a source of misclassification; added a discussion statement only.
steps.quote: While the analysis of the LIA is of interest, we have decided not to address this issue in the revision

steps.action: After RC1 (¶12) objected to the term perennial snow, renamed the classes to end-of-season snow-covered and start-of-season snow-free.
steps.quote: We renamed the perennial snow class to end-of-season snow-covered and the permanently snow-free class to start-of-season snow-free

steps.action: After RC3 (¶3, ¶28) found 'start of snowmelt' at the backscatter minimum ambiguous, redefined it as start of runoff in line with Marin et al. (2020).
steps.quote: Start of snowmelt (SOS) is now renamed as start of runoff (SOR), which is in line with Marin 2020 et al.

steps.action: After RC2 (¶2) and RC3 (¶3, ¶29) questioned dry-snow detection, narrowed the claim to snow cover depletion during melt, dropped the wet/dry distinction and added 'depletion' to the title.
steps.quote: Further, no differentiation between wet and dry snow is made anymore, as this is not the focus of our case study.

steps.action: After RC2 (¶5, ¶9) called the large-scale and pan-Arctic claims bold, toned down the abstract and the discussion statements.
steps.quote: Agree, we adjusted the statement accordingly.

steps.action: After RC2 (¶10) found the snow-depth explanation of the optimal threshold unsupported by data, withdrew the statement (it survives in hedged form in §5.2 ¶1).
steps.quote: Therefore, we have removed the statement.

steps.action: After RC3 (¶4) cited evidence of a cross-pol backscatter increase with dry snow accumulation, revised the Figure 1 schematic and the 'nearly transparent' statement.
steps.quote: You are correct, we have adjusted Figure 1 accordingly (increase during accumulation; potential lower snow-free maxima).

steps.action: Declined RC3 (¶5) request to investigate the drivers of regional differences in the backscatter increase (snow depth, substrate, topography, vegetation).
steps.quote: While this is definitely an interesting point, we have decided not to address this issue in the revision

steps.action: After RC3 (¶10), added the caveat that the 9 dB end-of-season criterion may not apply at other sites.
steps.quote: We have modified the statement accordingly.

steps.action: Prompted by RC3 (¶12), found that the exclusion of areas with SOD before 1 June was a mistake, removed it and reran the analysis; the authors report no significant change.
steps.quote: After cross-checking our analysis, we realized that this exclusion was unnecessary.

steps.action: After RC3 (¶14), stated the systematic differences between their threshold and Nagler's (threshold basis, sigma0 versus gamma0).
steps.quote: We mentioned the systematic differences between the two approaches now.

steps.action: Declined RC3 (¶20) suggestion to report Cohen's Kappa for class imbalance.
steps.quote: we decided to exclude Kappa and displayed the main results with a focus on the FP and TP rate

steps.action: After RC3 (¶23), replaced volume scattering with surface scattering and depolarization as the explanation of the HV increase.
steps.quote: We adjusted our statement accordingly.

steps.action: After RC3 (¶25) noted that no independent validation of the threshold was performed, stated earlier that the threshold-based assessment is weaker.
steps.quote: We agree with you that this should be mentioned earlier and have addressed that.

steps.action: After RC3 (¶7), labelled the algorithm empirical in the abstract.
steps.quote: Thank you for this suggestion. We have added this information.

steps.action: Declined RC4 (¶4) request to use SWE measurements to check that SOR is correctly identified.
steps.quote: So we decided to exclude SWE data.

steps.action: After RC4 (¶7) flagged that the SNAP terrain-flattening implementation is not correct per Small et al., noted this in the manuscript without reprocessing.
steps.quote: We were not aware of this and mention this now in the manuscript.

steps.action: Declined RC4 (¶8) request for measurements of surface roughness increase; no such data exist.
steps.quote: unfortunately, we do not have such data available for either of the two sites.

tree.answer: Seasonal SAR backscatter evolution during snowmelt and snow cover depletion
SC fraction observed directly only by local cameras; S-1 is indirect
Build and characterize an S-1 method for SC depletion and EOS
Marin's three causes of the increase; KRA: acquisition time vs snow distribution
Partly: timing of the rise relative to SOD separates snowpack change from SC fraction
Found: natural melt seasons at two monitored sites

tree.answer: Yes: two years at two sites
Threshold, polarization, derivative and second-site variation; optimum shifts by year and site
Survived after adding derivative and second site; several requests declined

end.claim: Sentinel-1 backscatter time series (HV, 4 dB global threshold, or the derivative) map SC depletion and EOS at 20 m and 6 d with overall SC map accuracy above 75 % (more than half of cases above 90 %) at two Greenland sites, against orthorectified time-lapse reference maps.

decisive_move.sentence: The same-day comparison of S-1 SC and EOS products with orthorectified time-lapse SC maps gives the accuracy figures; without it the method's performance would be uncharacterized.

gates.evidence: All available S-1 scenes and camera images were used; no hypothesis directed acquisition (§2.2 ¶1). The derivative products faced the camera reference without tuning to it, but the 4 dB threshold was chosen with the same reference used to assess it: 'The threshold-based product assessment is considered weaker as it was conducted with the same reference used for identifying this configuration' (§3.3.2 ¶1). No pre-fixed thresholds or analyses are reported; the 9 dB rule was set from observations (§3.1 ¶4).

imports.item: Discrete Fourier transform image registration (imreg_dft) to align time-lapse images
Receiver operating characteristic and confusion-matrix metrics for selecting threshold configurations
Off-the-shelf digital cameras (Canon EOS 1000D, HP Photosmart E427) as time-lapse sensors
Boxcar speckle filtering and range-Doppler terrain correction

novelty_claims.quote: [...] here present a novel empirical approach based on the temporal evolution of the SAR signal
We here propose a novel approach, which adapts Nagler’s method
With this new approach multiple advances are made compared to other recent studies on SAR-based SC detection
to the best of our knowledge, not presented with any other open-data remote sensing approach

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the backscatter-SC fraction interaction (snowpack change plus decreasing fractional SC drive the runoff-phase increase; the pre-SOD rise is absent in KRA because of faster, patchier melt) is best_explanation, with no roughness, grain or SWE data to test it (AC4 ¶54, ¶62). Transferability to other regions and vegetated areas is a stated expectation, not tested here (§6 ¶3). SOR is never validated, because the camera cannot detect it (§3.1 ¶6). The 4 dB threshold was selected and assessed on the same reference, so the threshold accuracy is in-sample. The derivative parameters (1 dB, 3 dB) and the 9 dB end-of-season rule are set without reported sensitivity tests; the end-of-season premise was checked only visually ('Visual assessment of the HV backscatter confirms', §3.1 ¶4). EOS agreement in KRA is poor (R2 below 0, §4.2 ¶4). The snow-depth explanation the authors said they removed (AC2 ¶63) persists in hedged form in §5.2 ¶1. The SNAP terrain-flattening issue was noted, not reprocessed (inference from AC4 ¶60). Code is available only on request. Composition: capability_first fits only loosely: the question and rivals precede the capability, and the walk is method building and validation against a reference, not exploration until a phenomenon repeats. The final_paper moves are coded from the published text, but the derivative approach and the Kobbefjord site were added only at referee request (review sequence).

disagreements.target: Nagler's method standard threshold (Nagler and Rott 2000; Nagler et al. 2016; Snapir et al. 2019)
disagreements.support: The 2-3 dB standard threshold rests on a different basis (dry-snow or snow-free reference versus seasonal minimum) and on sigma0 rather than gamma0, so the authors test a 2-10 dB range instead.
disagreements.quote: Using the standard threshold (2 to 3 dB) in Nagler's method might not be suited due to the different threshold basis

disagreements.target: Nagler's method as the current standard requiring reference images
disagreements.support: Using the full time series avoids selecting snow-free or dry-snow reference scenes, which end-of-season snow and firn can deteriorate.
disagreements.quote: we avoid the manual selection of reference images for Nagler’s method

disagreements.target: DEM-assisted and optical-assisted SAR snow mapping approaches
disagreements.support: From the literature: DEM-assisted methods overestimate dry snow in steep terrain, and optical inputs lower the spatiotemporal resolution.
disagreements.quote: these approaches cannot cover the small-scale heterogeneity of SC

disagreements.target: Tsai et al. (2019a, c) supervised classification of S-1 features
disagreements.support: Comparable accuracy in low-vegetation areas at 20 m rather than 100 m, with simpler, faster processing.
disagreements.quote: we keep the analysis fast and reduce processing capacity compared to the supervised classification approach by

disagreements.target: Marin et al. (2020) explanations of the runoff-phase backscatter increase
disagreements.support: Same-day camera SC fraction shows that part of the increase precedes any SC decrease (ZRA), so snowpack change and fractional SC both contribute.
disagreements.quote: is probably driven by changes in the snowpack, e.g., increased surface roughness, larger size and number of snow grains like suggested by

alternatives_considered.reason: The optimal threshold varies less in HV, so a global threshold performs better

alternatives_considered.alternatives: 2-8 dB (HV) and 2-10 dB (HH); season- and site-specific thresholds
alternatives_considered.reason: Best ROC response for both sites and years

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both threshold- and derivative-based EOS, with the derivative preferred
alternatives_considered.reason: The derivative needs no a priori knowledge or threshold optimization

alternatives_considered.chosen: Brightness histogram for camera snow classification
alternatives_considered.reason: To avoid misclassifying lakes and ponds reflecting the sky

alternatives_considered.chosen: Temporal filter (four acquisitions) without a spatial filter for the derivative
alternatives_considered.reason: To keep the 20 m spatial resolution; equal image count reduces S-1A/B differences

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Denser time series combining several S-1 orbits
alternatives_considered.reason: Different orbits differ in local incidence angle and acquisition time and must be analysed separately

alternatives_considered.chosen: Faster, more heterogeneous snow depletion explains the missing pre-SOD rise in KRA
alternatives_considered.reason: Shorter time for snowpack alteration and smaller patches; SOD-EOD duration differs between sites
